classification.difficultyReason: Discover the partition by shared endpoints and determine why each four-point set gives three line pairings while each three-point set gives three shared-endpoint choices.

content.prompt:
Consider $n$ distinct points arranged in a circle.

By considering the number of ways to choose 2 distinct lines that each pass through two of the points on the circle, show that
$$\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}=3\binom{n}{4}+3\binom{n}{3}.$$

answer.short:
$\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}=3\binom{n}{4}+3\binom{n}{3}$.

Four endpoints give three pairings; three endpoints give three choices of a shared point. These cases count every unordered pair of distinct lines.
answer.worked:
Each line is determined by two points, so there are $\binom{n}{2}$ lines and $\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}$ unordered pairs of distinct lines.

Alternatively, partition the pairs by their endpoints.

• No shared endpoint: choose four points in $\binom{n}{4}$ ways. Pair one fixed point with any of the other three; the remaining two form the second line. This gives $3\binom{n}{4}$ pairs.

• One shared endpoint: choose three points in $\binom{n}{3}$ ways, then choose their shared point in three ways. This gives $3\binom{n}{3}$ pairs.

These cases are disjoint and exhaustive, so
$$\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{2}=3\binom{n}{4}+3\binom{n}{3}.$$
